items.desc: A caring and supportive manager sounds like a dream for any employee, but could too much kindness turn "perfect" staff members into exhausted workaholics?

items.desc: Particles can generally move between neighboring sites in a crystal, a solid in which atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, or an optical lattice, an arrangement of laser-based traps that confines atoms. A strong potential gradient (i.e., a steep change in potential energy across a crystal or lattice) makes this ordinary particle hopping difficult and energetically costly.

items.title: California braces for triple flooding threat of huge tides, El Niño, warm oceans
items.desc: Exceptionally high tides and El Niño-fueled weather were threatening the California coast with possibly extreme flooding during the busiest U.S. travel week of the year.

items.title: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut set to board its space station
items.desc: China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft ahead of this week's launch, with a Pakistani set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its space station.

items.title: New quasar record tightens constraints on black hole formation scenarios
items.desc: A team of astronomers led by Julien Wolf, a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany (now at the European Southern Observatory in Garching bei München, Germany), discovered the most distant quasar to date. First identified in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the object was confirmed to be a quasar by subsequent observations with some of the most powerful telescopes on the ground and in space.

items.title: Funding must work better for SMEs to tackle energy challenges, finds research
items.desc: Scotland's small food and drink businesses face significant financial and operational barriers that could see them frozen out of vital funding to cut emissions from keeping produce cold, according to research from Heriot-Watt University.

items.title: Workplace absenteeism: Why temporary disability is a right, not an expense
items.desc: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.

items.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing
items.desc: Want to break down some basics in the world of quantum research over dinner? Researchers at the Cockrell School of Engineering have you covered.

items.title: AI has solved a host of big math problems—here's why this threatens the whole field of mathematics
items.desc: For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one when mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting-edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases.

items.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
items.desc: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

items.title: Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches
items.desc: Darwin's finches are known for their varied beaks, which help them take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Much previous research has focused on seed-eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention.

items.title: Recipe for one of the world's most important cancer drugs uncovered: Tobacco plants could produce the medicine
items.desc: More people around the world will receive a cancer diagnosis at some point in their lives. As this trend is expected to continue, researchers have been working to crack the code of how the widely used cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, with the aim of making its production cheaper and more efficient in the future.

items.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.desc: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?

items.title: Electron microscopy reveals the headquarters of poxviruses
items.desc: Mpox remains a smoldering threat, with recent clusters in Brazil, Thailand and Austria and ongoing hot spots across multiple African countries. Other poxviruses also endanger human or animal health. A new study by the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) uncovers the inner workings of the poxvirus core: how its gene-copying machines sit parked in dormant pairs, ready to print viral instructions and release them into the host cell through dedicated export portals embedded in the core shell.

items.title: Consumers, oblivious of being targeted, find online ads helpful
items.desc: Most online shoppers know that ads strategically follow them across sites, a mechanism known as "ad retargeting." A new study led by Penn State researchers found that consumers find these targeted ads helpful, but explaining why they are seeing an ad can backfire by increasing concerns about being watched.

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.desc: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.desc: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.desc: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
items.desc: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.desc: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
items.desc: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.desc: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
items.desc: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.desc: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.desc: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.desc: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry
items.desc: A surprising discovery at Brown University is challenging one of chemistry's most fundamental textbook explanations. Researchers found direct evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity changes how heavy atoms form triple bonds, causing normally distinct types of chemical bonds to blend together. The breakthrough confirms a decades-old prediction and suggests that traditional chemistry rules don't fully apply to heavy elements such as bismuth.

items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
items.desc: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

items.title: Is a Financial-Market Reckoning Imminent?
items.desc: After a year of unprecedented AI investment, increasingly financed by debt in opaque private markets, growing unease about the industry’s future is reflected in sharp declines in the NASDAQ index and the S&P 500. But the stock market’s dependence on a handful of highly leveraged companies—and even a single CEO—is hardly the only source of global financial risk. Amid mounting fears, we asked PS contributors what to expect from financial markets in the year ahead.

items.title: The African Union’s Elusive Quest for Security
items.desc: The African Union has long sought to implement Ali Mazrui’s concept of Pax Africana, but has faced persistent logistical and financial constraints. The key to making peacekeeping operations more effective is establishing a better division of labor between the AU, the United Nations, and regional African organizations.

items.title: The Achilles’ Heel of Emerging Economies’ Trade
items.desc: New research shows that 23% of global goods imports in 2024 faced at least two of three vulnerabilities: product criticality, supply concentration, and geopolitical distance. Given the wide range of problems, early diagnosis and targeted action are particularly important for emerging economies with limited fiscal space.

items.title: AI Agents Could Make Big Tech Bigger
items.desc: The rise of agentic AI could give a handful of Big Tech firms unprecedented power over our personal lives. Unless lawmakers and regulators act now, these digital gatekeepers could manipulate consumers, turbocharge corporate surveillance, and threaten our individual rights and civil liberties.

items.title: If the AI Bubble Is Bursting, the Fallout Will Be Severe
items.desc: With the S&P 500 following the tech-heavy NASDAQ into correction territory, even as Anthropic set a record with its initial public offering, this is a good moment to compare AI stock valuations with earlier asset-price bubbles. A look back at the dot-com boom and bust of the late 1990s offers ample cause for concern.

items.title: Journalism Can Be More Than AI Fodder
items.desc: As AI fundamentally alters the information environment, news publishers risk becoming little more than content suppliers for Big Tech. To avoid that fate, many are drawing on their archives and expertise to develop AI tools that allow them to operate and compete on their own terms.

items.title: Governing African Economies as They Are
items.desc: Africa cannot overcome its development challenges by applying the same knowledge, economic, and innovation systems that helped create them. Imagining and governing new ways forward will require three intellectual ruptures.

items.title: Making Earth Cool Again
items.desc: Climate multilateralism is evolving into a two-tiered system in which high-level negotiations toward shared commitments and the real-world implementation of climate solutions become more mutually supportive. Only by unleashing such virtuous cycles can we keep the 1.5ºC target for global warming within reach.

items.title: America’s Lame-Duck Autocrat
items.desc: When autocrats suffer a defeat, they tend to double down, such as by intensifying repression at home or behaving more recklessly abroad. With two years left in office after historic midterm election losses, this is the road US President Donald Trump appears to be taking.

items.title: Getting Ukraine’s House in Order
items.desc: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly opposed the idea of forming a national unity government. But bringing opposition leaders into the cabinet would ensure the checks on corruption and wayward bureaucratic action that Zelensky’s team can no longer provide.

items.title: What Adam Smith Missed
items.desc: For all that he got right, the "founding father" of economics failed to see how technological innovations lead to market monopolization. If AI is left to the invisible hand, it will almost certainly increase economic and political inequality, causing even deeper social polarization and further undermining democracy.

items.title: China Ratchets Up Its Weaponization of Trade
items.desc: Just as the US has been leveraging its large market and technological leadership for geopolitical ends, China is now using its dominance in critical minerals, industrial inputs, and specialized manufacturing machinery to coerce and punish other countries. The consequences, both economic and geopolitical, are far-reaching.

items.title: There Is Only One Thing to Talk About With Russia
items.desc: The European security order’s foundational principle is never to tolerate aggression. There is no need to revise that order, as the Kremlin has proposed, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to respect other countries’ territorial integrity and uphold its own previous commitments.

items.title: The Truth About Global AI Governance
items.desc: Because the current approach to global AI governance presumes that developing countries are full of eager adopters of AI who need to be cautioned about the technology's risks, it overlooks what their information environments and media markets actually need. A survey of researchers who study 71 countries sets the record straight.

items.title: Demography is the Achilles’ Heel of Dictatorships
items.desc: Governments that manipulate population figures often end up deceiving themselves as much as the public. When autocratic leaders mistake inflated numbers for real national strength, they make costly strategic mistakes and fail to address their countries’ demographic decline until it is too late.

items.title: Judge the Cyber Apocalypse by the Data, Not the Headlines
items.desc: The technical metrics on AI for cybersecurity now indicate that recent advances are enabling attackers more than defenders and that AI is regularly being used in attacks. This is in line with daily news stories on the “vulnpocalypse” and “Black October.” Surprisingly though, data on real-world impacts of cyber attacks tells a less dire story. If this trend continues, it could indicate that attribution and punishment matter at least as much as attackers’ technical capabilities. items.title: Biodata Matters for the Genesis Mission
items.desc: The Genesis Mission aims to harness artificial intelligence to supercharge scientific innovation and support the United States’ technological leadership, including in biotechnology. This piece describes the categories of biodata challenges that the Genesis Mission is likely to face and makes recommendations about how to approach them. items.title: Convergent Interests: How America Could Undermine Its Own AI Advantage
items.desc: A convergence of political, commercial, and ideological pressures can impede America’s AI leadership, and public controversies are powerful enough to catalyze that convergence. Our piece spotlights this issue, urging policymakers to govern AI responsibly without disabling the innovation that makes American leadership possible—even in the wake of scandal. items.desc: CSET’s Hanna Dohmen and Sam Bresnick shared their expert analysis in an op-ed published by Barron’s. The article examines how Nvidia’s recent scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang could lead to stricter U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips. items.title: AI Kill Switches: What Policymakers Should Know
items.desc: Policymakers have recently proposed requiring “AI kill switches” to quickly stop an AI system or limit the impact of a harmful or unwanted AI incident. This piece describes different potential implementations of AI kill switches at each layer of the AI stack and offers key takeaways for policymakers. The post AI Kill Switches: What Policymakers Should Know appeared first on Center for Security and Emerging Technology .

items.title: Espionage, AI, and the Risks of Strategic Overreaction
items.desc: Allegations involving Nvidia’s chief executive have renewed scrutiny of Chinese intelligence collection and U.S. controls on advanced AI chips.
